A '''mandarin orange''' ('''''Citrus reticulata'''''), often simply called '''mandarin''', is a small, rounded [[citrus]] tree [[fruit]]. Treated as a distinct species of [[Orange (fruit) |orange]], it is usually eaten plain or in [[Fruit salad|fruit salads.]] The mandarin is small and oblate, unlike the roughly spherical sweet orange (which is a mandarin-[[pomelo]] [[Hybrid (biology) |hybrid]]). The [[taste]] is sweeter and stronger than the common orange. A ripe mandarin orange is firm to slightly soft, heavy for its size, and pebbly-skinned. The peel is thin and loose, with little white [[mesocarp]], so they are usually easier to peel and to split into segments. Hybrids have these traits to lesser degrees. The mandarin orange is tender and is damaged easily by cold. It can be grown in tropical and subtropical areas.

According to genetic studies, the wild mandarin was one of the [[Citrus taxonomy#Ancestral species |original citrus species]]; through breeding or natural hybridization, it is the ancestor of many [[Citrus taxonomy#Hybrids |hybrid citrus]] cultivars. With the [[citron]] and pomelo, it is the ancestor of the most commercially important hybrids. Though the ancestral mandarin orange was bitter, most commercial mandarin strains derive from hybridization with the pomelo, which gives them sweet fruit.

== Etymology ==

The name ''mandarin orange'' is a [[calque]] of Swedish ''mandarin apelsin'' [''apelsin'' from German ''Apfelsine'' (''Apfel'' + ''[[Names of China |Sina]]''), meaning ''Chinese apple''], first attested in the 18th century. The Imperial Chinese term "mandarine" was first adopted by the [[French language |French]] for this fruit. The reason for the epithet is not clear.<ref>{{cite web |last=De La Cruz-Cabanillas |first=Isabel |date=1 January 2008 |title=Chinese loanwords in the OED |url=https://www.thefreelibrary.com/Chinese+loanwords+in+the+OED.-a0194473142 |access-date=October 5, 2016 |work=[[The Free Library]] |publisher=Farlex, Inc}}</ref>

''Citrus reticulata'' is from Latin, where reticulata means "netted".<ref name="mbg">{{cite web |date=2019 |title=''Citrus reticulata'' 'Clementine' |url=http://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=244327 |access-date=8 March 2019 |website=Plant Finder |publisher=Missouri Botanical Garden}}</ref>

== Description ==

=== Tree ===

[[File:Mandarinier Gortyne.jpg|thumb|Fruiting mandarin tree in [[Crete]] ]]

''Citrus reticulata'' is a moderate-sized tree some {{convert |25 |ft |meter |order=flip}} in height.<ref name=mbg/><ref name=morton/> The tree trunk and major branches have thorns. The leaves are shiny, green, and rather small. The [[petiole (botany) |petioles]] are short, almost wingless or slightly winged. The flowers are borne singly or in small groups in the leaf-axils.<ref name=morton/> Citrus are usually [[self-fertile]] (needing only a [[bee]] to move [[pollen]] within the same flower) or [[parthenocarpic]] (not needing [[pollination]] and therefore seedless, such as the [[Citrus unshiu|satsuma]]). A mature mandarin tree can yield up to {{convert |175 |lbs |kg |order=flip}} of fruit.<ref name="ucr">{{cite web |date=2010 |title=Tango mandarin; ''Citrus reticulata'' Blanco |url=https://citrusvariety.ucr.edu/citrus/tango.html |access-date=8 March 2019 |website=Citrus Variety Collection |publisher=College of Natural and Agricultural Sciences, [[University of California Riverside]]}}</ref>

=== Fruit ===

Mandarin orange fruits are small {{convert|40|-|80|mm|in|sp=us}}.<ref name=morton/> Their color is [[orange (colour) |orange]], yellow-orange, or red-orange.<ref name=karp/> The skin is thin and peels off easily.<ref name=morton/> Their easiness to peel is an important advantage of mandarin oranges over other citrus fruits.<ref name=karp/> Just like with other citrus fruits, mandarin is separated easily from the segments.<ref name=morton/> The fruits may be [[seedless]] or contain a small number of [[seed]]s. Though the ancestral mandarin orange was bitter, most commercial mandarin strains derive from hybridization with pomelo, which gives them sweet fruit.<ref name="Wang"/> They can be eaten as whole or squeezed to make [[juice]].<ref name=morton/><ref name=karp/> A ripe mandarin orange is firm to slightly soft, heavy for its size, and pebbly-skinned. The peel is thin and loose, with little white [[mesocarp]], so they are easy to peel and to split into segments.<ref name="latimes">{{cite news |last=Karp |first=David |date=13 March 2014 |title=Market watch: The wild and elusive Dancy |newspaper=[[Los Angeles Times]] |url=https://www.latimes.com/food/la-fo-marketwatch-20110128-story.html |access-date=7 February 2019}}</ref>

{{further|Citrus taxonomy|Mandarin orange varieties}}

=== Domestication ===
Mandarins appear to have been domesticated at least twice, in the north and south [[Nanling Mountains]], derived from separate wild subspecies. Wild mandarins are still found there, including Daoxian mandarines (sometimes given the species name ''Citrus daoxianensis'') as well as some members of the group traditionally called 'Mangshan wild mandarins', a generic grouping for the wild mandarin-like fruit of the Mangshan area that includes both true mandarins (''mangshanyeju'',<ref name=Wu2021>{{cite journal |title=Diversification of mandarin citrus by hybrid speciation and apomixis |last1=Wu |first1=Guohong Albert |last2=Sugimoto |first2=Chikatoshi |last3=Kinjo |first3=Hideyasu |last4=Asama |first4=Chika |last5=Mitsube |first5=Fumimasa |last6=Talon |first6=Manuel |last7=Gmitter |first7=Grederick G Jr |last8=Rokhsar |first8=Daniel S |journal=[[Nature Communications]] |date=2021 |volume=12 |issue=1 |page=4377 |doi=10.1038/s41467-021-24653-0 |pmid=34312382 |pmc=8313541 |bibcode=2021NatCo..12.4377W |doi-access=free}} and Supplement</ref> the southern subspecies) and the genetically distinct and only distantly-related [[Mangshanyegan]]. The wild mandarins were found free of the introgressed pomelo (''C. maxima'') DNA found in domestic mandarins. Still, they did appear to have small amounts (~1.8%) of introgression from the [[Citrus ichangensis |ichang papeda]], which grows wild in the same region.<ref name="Wang2018">{{cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=Lun |display-authors=etal |title=Genome of Wild Mandarin and Domestication History of Mandarin |journal=Molecular Plant |volume=11 |number=8 |pages=1024–1037 |year=2018 |doi=10.1016/j.molp.2018.06.001 |pmid=29885473 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

The Nanling Mountains are home to northern and southern genetic clusters of domestic mandarins that have similar levels of sugars in the fruit compared to their wild relatives but appreciably (in some almost 90-fold) lower levels of citric acid. The clusters display different patterns of pomelo introgression, have different deduced historical population histories, and are most closely related to distinct wild mandarins, suggesting two independent domestications in the north and south. All tested domesticated cultivars belong to one of these two genetic clusters, with varieties such as Nanfengmiju, Kishu, and Satsuma from the northern domestication event producing larger, redder fruit, while varieties such as Willowleaf, Dancy, Sunki, Cleopatra, King, and Ponkan belong to the smaller, yellower-fruited southern cluster.<ref name="Wang2018"/>

=== Taxonomy ===
The [[Citrus taxonomy |Tanaka classification system]] divided domestic mandarins and similar fruit into numerous species, giving distinct names to cultivars such as willowleaf mandarins (''C. deliciosa''), [[satsuma (fruit) |satsuma]]s (''C. unshiu''), [[tangerines]] (''C. tangerina''). Under the [[Citrus taxonomy |Swingle system]], all these are considered to be varieties of a single species, ''Citrus reticulata''.<ref name=identification /> Hodgson represented them as several subgroups: common (''C. reticulata''), Satsuma, [[Citrus nobilis |King]] (''C. nobilis''), Mediterranean (willowleaf), small-fruited (''C. indica'', ''C. tachibana'' and ''C. reshni''), and mandarin hybrids.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Goldenberg |first1=Livnat |last2=Yaniv |first2=Yossi |last3=Porat |first3=Ron |last4=Carmi |first4=Nir |title=Mandarin fruit quality: a review |journal=Journal of the Science of Food and Agriculture |volume=98 |issue=1 |pages=18–26 |year=2018 |doi=10.1002/jsfa.8495 |pmid=28631804 |bibcode=2018JSFA...98...18G }}</ref> In the genomic-based species taxonomy of Ollitrault et al., only pure wild type mandarins would fall under ''C. reticulata'', while the pomelo admixture found in the majority of mandarins would cause them to be classified as varieties of the hybrid bitter orange, ''C. aurantium''.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Ollitrault |first1=Patrick |chapter=Citrus taxonomy |date=2020 |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/B9780128121634000048 |title=The Genus Citrus |pages=57–81 |publisher=Elsevier |doi=10.1016/b978-0-12-812163-4.00004-8 |isbn=978-0-12-812163-4 |access-date=2021-01-17 |last2=Curk |first2=Franck |last3=Krueger |first3=Robert |s2cid=242819146}}</ref>

Genetic analysis is consistent with continental mandarins representing a single species, varying due to hybridization.<ref name="Wu Terol Ibanez 2018"/> An island species, ''[[Citrus ryukyuensis]]'' that diverged 2 to 3 million years ago when cut off by rising sea levels, was found on [[Okinawa Island]]. Its hybridization with the mainland species has produced unique island cultivars in Japan and Taiwan, such as the [[Tachibana orange]]<ref name=Wu2021/> the [[Shekwasha]],<ref name=Wu2021/> and [[Nanfengmiju]].<ref name="auto">{{cite news |last=Karp |first=David |date=13 January 2010 |title=The Seedless Kishu, a small but mighty mandarin |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |url=https://www.latimes.com/food/la-fow-marketwatch8-2010jan13-story.html |access-date=17 January 2021}}</ref> They have some pomelo DNA, like all domesticated mandarins.<ref name="Wang2018"/> Northern and southern domesticates contain different pomelo contributions.<ref name="Wang2018"/> An 'acidic' group including Sunki and [[Cleopatra mandarin]]s  likewise contain small regions of [[introgression|introgressed]] pomelo DNA; they are too sour to eat, but are widely used as rootstock and grown for juice.<ref name=identification>{{cite journal |doi=10.1007/s11295-010-0314-x |volume=7 |title=New universal mitochondrial PCR markers reveal new information on maternal citrus phylogeny |journal= Tree Genetics & Genomes |pages=49–61 |year=2011 |last1=Froelicher |first1=Yann |last2=Mouhaya |first2=Wafa |last3=Bassene |first3=Jean-Baptiste |last4=Costantino |first4=Gilles |last5=Kamiri |first5=Mourad |last6=Luro |first6=Francois |last7=Morillon |first7=Raphael |last8=Ollitrault |first8=Patrick |display-authors=5 |s2cid=32371305 |url=http://agritrop.cirad.fr/558353/ |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="Wu Terol Ibanez 2018"/> Another group, including some tangerines, satsuma, and king mandarins, show more pomelo contribution.<ref name="Wu Terol Ibanez 2018"/> Hybrid mandarins thus fall on a continuum of increasing pomelo contribution with clementines, sweet and sour oranges, and grapefruit.<ref name="Curk"/><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Klein |first1=Joshua D. |volume=2 |pages=199–214 |doi=10.1007/978-94-017-9276-9_10 |series=Medicinal and Aromatic Plants of the World |year=2014 |title=Medicinal and Aromatic Plants of the Middle-East |isbn=978-94-017-9275-2 |chapter=Citron Cultivation, Production and Uses in the Mediterranean Region}}</ref><ref name="Wu Terol Ibanez 2018">{{cite journal |last1=Wu |first1=Guohong Albert |last2=Terol |first2=Javier |last3=Ibanez |first3=Victoria |last4=López-García |first4=Antonio |last5=Pérez-Román |first5=Estela |last6=Borredá |first6=Carles |last7=Domingo |first7=Concha |last8=Tadeo |first8=Francisco R. |last9=Carbonell-Caballero |first9=Jose |last10=Alonso |first10=Roberto |last11=Curk |first11=Franck |last12=Du |first12=Dongliang |last13=Ollitrault |first13=Patrick |last14=Roose |first14=Mikeal L. == Production ==
In 2024, world production of mandarin oranges (combined with tangerines and clementines in reporting to [[FAOSTAT]]) was approximately 50 million [[tonne]]s, led by China with 51% of the total.<ref name="faostat">{{cite web |date=2026 |title=Mandarin orange production in 2024 (includes tangerines and clementines) from pick lists: World regions/Production quantity/Crops/Year |url=https://www.fao.org/faostat/en/#data/QCL |access-date=24 April 2026 |publisher=FAOSTAT, United Nations Corporate Statistical Database}}</ref> [[Turkey]] produced two million tonnes in 2024, with [[Spain]] and [[Egypt]] as other significant producers.<ref name=faostat/>

=== Culinary ===
{{See also |List of fruit dishes}}

Mandarins have a stronger and sweeter taste than sweet oranges.<ref name="karp">{{cite news |author=Karp |first=David |date=3 February 2016 |title=Mandarin oranges, rising stars of the fruit bowl |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/02/03/dining/mandarin-orange.html |access-date=7 February 2019}}</ref> They are peeled and eaten fresh or used in salads, desserts and main dishes.<ref name="morton">{{cite web |author=Morton |first=Julia F. |date=1987 |title=Mandarin orange; In: Fruits of Warm Climates, p. 142–145 |url=https://www.hort.purdue.edu/newcrop/morton/mandarin_orange.html |access-date=8 March 2019 |website=New Crop Resource Online Program |publisher=Center for New Crops and Plant Products, Purdue University}}</ref> Fresh mandarins are used in the production of the [[liqueur]] [[Mandarine Napoléon]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Mandarine Napoléon - History |url=https://www.mandarinenapoleon.com/history/ |website=[[Mandarine Napoléon]] |date=23 May 2018 |access-date=23 September 2023}}</ref>

The [[peel (fruit) |peel]] is used fresh, whole or [[zest (ingredient)|as zest]], or dried as [[chenpi]]. It can be used as a spice for cooking, baking, drinks, or candy. [[Essential oil]] from the fresh peel may be used as a flavoring for candy, in [[gelatin]]s, [[ice cream]], [[chewing gum]], and baked goods.<ref name=morton/> It is used as a flavoring in some liqueurs.<ref name=morton/>

== Fruit rind oil ==
[[File:Citrus reticulata (Mandarine) 1.jpg|thumb|Mandarin with oil glands in the bark]]
The oils expressed from the peel/rind of mandarin are used as flavor and fragrance materials. Compositional differences arise from both cultivar<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lota |first1=Marie-Laure |title=Chemical variability of peel and leaf essential oils of mandarins from Citrus reticulata Blanco |journal=Biochemical Systematics and Ecology |date=January 2000 |volume=28 |issue=1 |page=61 |doi=10.1016/S0305-1978(99)00036-8 |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0305197899000368|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and stage of fruit ripeness<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bhuyan |first1=Namita |title=Physico-chemical variation in peel oils of Khasi mandarin (Citrus reticulata Blanco) during ripening |journal=Indian Journal of Plant Physiology |date=2015 |volume=20 |page=227 |doi=10.1007/s40502-015-0164-5 |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40502-015-0164-5|url-access=subscription }}</ref> (green<ref>{{cite web |title=Mandarin Oil, Green |url=https://fraterworks.com/products/mandarin-oil-green |website=Fraterworks.com |publisher=Fraterworks |access-date=3 April 2026}}</ref> - unripe; yellow<ref>{{cite web |title=Mandarin Oil, Yellow|url=https://fraterworks.com/products/mandarin-oil-yellow|website=Fraterworks.com |publisher=Fraterworks |access-date=3 April 2026}}</ref> - partially ripe; and "red"<ref>{{cite web |title=Mandarin Oil, Red|url=https://fraterworks.com/products/mandarin-oil-red|website=Fraterworks.com |publisher=Fraterworks |access-date=3 April 2026}}</ref> - fully ripe). In general, the aroma of the peel oils are described as "citrus, floral, bitter orange, orange, terpenic, aldehydic, orange rind, neroli".<ref>{{cite web |title=mandarin oil|url=https://scentsandflavors.com/database/9dbb4b09-7b68-4248-accc-67c7d83a4a7d|website=Scents and Flavors |publisher=Scents and Flavors |access-date=3 April 2026}}</ref>

== Cultural significance ==

In North America, mandarins are commonly purchased in 5- or 10-pound boxes,<ref name=karp/> individually wrapped in soft green paper, and given in [[Christmas stocking]]s. This custom goes back to the 1880s when Japanese immigrants in Canada and the United States began receiving Japanese mandarin oranges from their families back home as gifts for the New Year. The tradition spread among the non-Japanese population and eastwards across the country: each November harvest, "The oranges were quickly unloaded and shipped east by rail. 'Orange Trains' – trains with boxcars painted orange – alerted everyone along the way that the irresistible oranges from Japan were back again for the holidays. For many, the arrival of Japanese mandarin oranges signalled the beginning of the holiday season."<ref name=AITC1>{{cite web |title=Information on This Week's Product: Mandarin Oranges |url=http://www.aitc.ca/bc/uploads/sfvnp/MANDARIN%20ORANGES%206.pdf |publisher=BC Agriculture in the Classroom Foundation |access-date=24 January 2013 |archive-date=1 February 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160201060025/http://www.aitc.ca/bc/uploads/sfvnp/MANDARIN%20ORANGES%206.pdf}}</ref> Satsumas were grown in the United States from the early 1900s. Still, Japan remained a major supplier.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Andersen |first1=Peter C. |last2=Ferguson |first2=James J. |date=19 November 2014 |title=The Satsuma Mandarin |url=http://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/ch116 |access-date=9 April 2018 |website=Electronic Data Information Source |publisher=IFAS Extension, University of Florida}}</ref> U.S. imports of these Japanese oranges was suspended due to hostilities with Japan during World War II.<ref name="AITC1" /> While they were one of the first Japanese goods allowed for export after the end of the war, residual hostility led to the rebranding of these oranges as "Mandarin" oranges instead of "Japanese" oranges.<ref name="AITC1"/> 

The delivery of the first batch of mandarin oranges from Japan in the port of [[Vancouver]] is greeted with a festival that combines Santa Claus and Japanese dancers<ref name="Marion" />—young girls dressed in traditional [[kimono]]s.<ref name="France-CanadaChristmas">{{cite web |title=Christmas Stockings |url=http://www.culture.gouv.fr/culture/noel/angl/basnoel.htm |work=Christmas Traditions in France and in Canada |publisher=Ministère de la culture et de la communication de France |access-date=15 January 2013}}</ref> Historically, the Christmas fruit sold in North America was mostly [[Dancy (fruit) |Dancys]], but now it is more often a hybrid.<ref name="arkoftaste">{{Cite web |date=2014 |title=Ark of Taste, Dancy Tangerine, ''Citrus Tangerina v. Dancy'' |url=http://www.slowfoodusa.org/ark-item/dancy-tangerine |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140712213717/http://www.slowfoodusa.org/ark-item/dancy-tangerine |archive-date=12 July 2014 |access-date=17 January 2021 |website=Slow Food USA}}</ref> This Japanese tradition merged with European traditions related to the [[Christmas stocking]]. [[Saint Nicholas]] is said to have put [[gold]] coins into the stockings of three poor girls so that they would be able to afford to get married.<ref name="AFP">{{cite web |date=4 October 2008 |title=Personalized Christmas Stockings |url=http://www.centrinet.com/christmas/catclas.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081021102047/http://www.centrinet.com/christmas/catclas.htm |archive-date=21 October 2008 |access-date=15 January 2013 |work=Stocking Factory}}</ref> Sometimes the story is told with gold balls instead of bags of gold, and oranges became a symbolic stand-in for these gold balls, and are put in Christmas stockings in Canada.<ref name="AFP" /><ref name="Marion">{{cite web |last=Marion |first=Paul |date=19 December 2010 |title=Oranges at Christmas |url=http://www.richardhowe.com/2010/12/19/oranges-at-christmas/ |access-date=15 January 2013 |website=Richard Howe; Lowell Politics and Lowell History}}</ref> Their use as Christmas gifts probably spread from the Japanese immigrant community.<ref name="coop">{{cite web |title=CPW Celebrates 20 Years of Churchill Orchard's Kishu Mandarin Magic |url=https://www.cpw.coop/cpw-blog/kishu-20th |website=Co-op Partners Warehouse |access-date=27 October 2024 |date=24 January 2024}}</ref> Mandarin oranges are mentioned in [[Sinclair Ross]]' 1942 novel, ''[[As for Me and My House]]'', and his 1939 short story, ''Cornet at Night''.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Boyd |first1=Shelley |last2=Cooke |first2=Nathalie |last3=Moyer |first3=Alexia |date=2020-02-01 |title=A literary history of the Mandarin orange in Canada |url=https://online.ucpress.edu/gastronomica/article-abstract/20/1/83/109141/A-Literary-History-of-the-Mandarin-Orange-in?redirectedFrom=fulltext |journal=Gastronomica|volume=20 |issue=1 |pages=83–89 |doi=10.1525/gfc.2020.20.1.83 |doi-access=free|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
